clue.text: An ordinary girl gives the smallest possible amount

parts.note: Penny is a girl's name
a farthing was the lowest-value old British coin, a quarter of a penny, so it stands for a tiny sum

explanation.surface: A plain young woman hands over the tiniest sum she can manage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ordinary' looks like an adjective for the girl, but the 'ordinary' was the Victorian name for the high-wheeled bicycle.
explanation.definitionFit: The high-wheeled Victorian bicycle was called an ordinary before the safety bicycle replaced it.

clue.text: Figures corresponding to weightlessness

parts.note: parallel means corresponding or analogous
having no weight is weighing zero grams, O standing for zero

explanation.surface: Numbers that match a state of floating in space.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Figures' suggests numbers, but these are geometric shapes.
explanation.definitionFit: Parallelograms are four-sided shapes in geometry, plane figures.

clue.text: Slow mover's beginning to come last, taking big tacks

indicators.note: the opening letter of the slow creature's name moves round to the end

parts.note: a snail is the proverbial slow mover

explanation.surface: A snail's journey starts late as it takes on some large drawing pins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beginning to come last' moves the S of SNAIL to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Nails are metal spikes for fastening, larger relatives of tacks.

clue.text: Villon's snow date

parts.note: the poet François Villon asked where the snows of a time long past had gone, in a refrain famous in Rossetti's translation

explanation.surface: When the French poet's snow fell.
explanation.walkthrough: Rossetti's translation of Villon's ballade asks 'But where are the snows of ...?', naming a vanished past.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means times gone by, the season the poet's vanished snows belonged to.

clue.text: A service a journalist compiled

parts.note: taken as written
Mass is a church service
ed is short for editor, a journalist

explanation.surface: A newspaper writer assembled a religious service.
explanation.definitionFit: To amass is to gather or accumulate, much as one collects material to compile it.

clue.text: High position given to Peter maybe

indicators.note: maybe suggests the letters of to and Peter could be arranged another way

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone called Peter is promoted to a lofty post.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maybe' rearranges TO and PETER together.
explanation.definitionFit: The top of a tree is a lofty perch, a high position.

clue.text: A short distance from the island

explanation.surface: Just a little way off the island.
explanation.definitionFit: An inch is a small unit of length; in Scotland and Ireland an inch is also a small island.

clue.text: Kitchen girl, say, in port

indicators.note: say tells us to go by how the phrase is pronounced

parts.note: a galley is a ship's kitchen and Polly is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A scullery maid, for example, at the docks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kitchen girl' suggests a scullery maid; it is GALLEY plus POLLY. Gallipoli is a port on the Dardanelles in Turkey.
explanation.definitionFit: Gallipoli (Gelibolu) is a Turkish harbour town on the Dardanelles, a port.

clue.text: Eggheads let one sign in late, oddly enough

indicators.note: oddly enough hints that the letters come in a strange order and must be rearranged

parts.note: one is I in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Intellectuals allow someone to register after the deadline, which is strange.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly enough' rearranges LET, I, SIGN, IN and LATE.
explanation.definitionFit: Eggheads are clever people, and the intelligentsia are the intellectual class.

clue.text: Put back to control the country

parts.note: to rein is to control, as a rider does a horse
a state is a nation or country

explanation.surface: Someone is returned to office to govern the nation.
explanation.definitionFit: To restore someone to a former place or role is to put them back.

clue.text: Stop an officer performing

parts.note: Col is the abbreviation for colonel, an army officer
a performer is on, that is, on stage

explanation.surface: An order to halt a military man in the middle of his act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stop' is a punctuation mark here, not an order to halt.
explanation.definitionFit: A colon is a punctuation mark, and such marks are traditionally called stops.

clue.text: Stocking maker in the City without transport

annotationWithheld.why: Stocking maker in the City without transport: LISLE fits 'Stocking maker' (lisle thread; Lisle is the old spelling of Lille), but no reading of 'in the City without transport' builds the letters
annotationWithheld.clue: Stocking maker in the City without transport

clue.text: This place makes sound sense

indicators.note: the word sound in the clue tells us to go by how a word is pronounced

parts.note: sight is one of the five senses

explanation.surface: A remark that this location is a sensible one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sound' looks like an adjective meaning sensible, but it is the signal to go by pronunciation.
explanation.definitionFit: A site is a location or plot, a synonym for place.

clue.text: Subtle punishment

explanation.surface: A gentle kind of penalty.
explanation.definitionFit: Fine as an adjective means delicate or nuanced; as a noun it is a money penalty imposed for an offence.

clue.text: Heard plainsong out of Holst's last heavenly presentations

indicators.note: the final letter of the composer's name sits within, with the rest coming out of it on both sides
heard tells us to use what the words sound like

parts.note: read as plain plus song, which is plain aria and sounds like plane aria

indicators.note: last points to the final letter of Holst

explanation.surface: Chant was heard emerging from the end of a Holst work about the heavens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plainsong' is one word but must be read as two, plain and song. 'out of' puts Holst's final letter between the two parts. Holst composed The Planets, which ties in with the heavenly theme.
explanation.definitionFit: Planetaria are domed theatres projecting the night sky, so they put on shows of the heavens.

clue.text: Girl in need perhaps of being appreciated

indicators.note: the word in tells us the girl's name is placed within the other letters
perhaps hints that the word need is not in its final arrangement and must be rearranged

parts.note: Joy is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A young woman who is in want, possibly from lack of recognition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges the clue word need, and 'in' places the girl inside the shuffled letters. 'Girl in need' reads as a hard-luck story.
explanation.definitionFit: If something was liked and relished, it was appreciated.

clue.text: The middle of a song is omitted in this dive

annotationWithheld.why: The middle of a song is omitted in this dive: the song wanted is 'Mack the Knife' less THE, which gives MACKKNIFE, not JACKKNIFE; no reading of the clue as held gives the J
annotationWithheld.clue: The middle of a song is omitted in this dive

clue.text: Bribe to give the Victory sign — it helps the revolution

parts.note: a palm branch was the classical emblem of victory
oil lubricates turning wheels and axles, helping them revolve

explanation.surface: A protester is paid off to flash a V-sign in support of the uprising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolution' suggests politics, but it is the turning of a wheel, which oil makes easier.
explanation.definitionFit: Palm oil is slang for a bribe, money pressed into someone's palm.

clue.text: Food producer is pitiless with killer whale

parts.note: orc is an old name for the orca or killer whale
hard means unfeeling or pitiless

explanation.surface: A grower who is as ruthless as an orca.
explanation.definitionFit: A plot of fruit trees yields apples, pears and so on, so it produces food.

clue.text: Forceful Radical

explanation.surface: A strong and extreme measure.
explanation.definitionFit: Drastic measures are severe and powerful, and also extreme or sweeping in effect.

clue.text: Preserving the Viceroy

explanation.surface: A note about keeping the governor of India in good condition.
explanation.definitionFit: Canning keeps food in sealed tins; Lord Canning was the first Viceroy of British India, from 1858.

clue.text: Watch small jazz band outside in Asian capital

indicators.note: outside tells us the band's letters go around the other word

parts.note: a combo is a small group of jazz musicians
lo is an old exclamation meaning look or watch

explanation.surface: Seeing a little jazz group playing out of doors in an Asian city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Watch' suggests a timepiece, but it is LO, as in 'lo and behold'. Colombo was the capital of Sri Lanka.
explanation.definitionFit: Colombo is the chief city of Sri Lanka and was long its capital.

clue.text: Roué causes sailor to lose his head

indicators.note: losing a head means the first letter of the word for the sailor is dropped

parts.note: Sir Francis Drake was the famous Elizabethan sailor

explanation.surface: A seducer drives a seaman to distraction.
explanation.walkthrough: The OCR dropped the accent letter of 'Roué'. 'Lose his head' suggests panic, but it removes the D from DRAKE.
explanation.definitionFit: A roué is a debauched man, a libertine, which a rake also is.

clue.text: Assembly meeting nearly every day?

indicators.note: nearly means the word for every day is used without its final letter

parts.note: daily means every day

explanation.surface: A question whether a gathering convenes almost daily.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dáil is the lower house of the Irish parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dáil is the elected chamber of Ireland's legislature, a parliamentary assembly.

clue.text: Cards in stock total only a bit more than half

indicators.note: the run taken from the words total only is five of their nine letters, a little over half of them, lying inside

explanation.surface: Playing cards held in reserve add up to barely more than half the pack.
explanation.walkthrough: In card games the talon is the undealt stock pile.
explanation.definitionFit: The talon is the pile of undealt cards left after the deal, the stock.

clue.text: Such a pocket contains money

parts.note: the phrase about someone profiting is to have the pockets so filled, as cloth backs a pocket, here with cash

explanation.surface: A remark about a pocket with cash in it.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'line one's pockets' is to make money, often dishonestly.
explanation.definitionFit: A pocket full of money is said to be filled inside with it, as fabric backs a coat.

clue.text: Auditor's books about one inside

indicators.note: inside tells us one letter is placed within the others

parts.note: OT is the Old Testament, books of the Bible
c is short for circa, meaning about
one is I in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: An accountant's ledgers contain a single item.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Auditor' suggests an accountant checking books, but it means a listener.
explanation.definitionFit: Otic means relating to the ear, and an auditor is a listener.

clue.text: Rainy month is August latterly

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: latterly points to the end of the word August, its final letter

explanation.surface: August, at its end, turns out to be a wet month.
explanation.definitionFit: Damp weather is wet, as rainy weather is.

clue.text: Fruit gives doctor stamina, surprisingly

indicators.note: surprisingly hints that these letters come out in an unexpected order

explanation.surface: A piece of fruit gives a physician unexpected staying power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'surprisingly' rearranges DR plus STAMINA.
explanation.definitionFit: Tamarinds are tropical pods with edible sour pulp, a kind of fruit.

clue.text: One can cope with delay in order to get a book of reference

indicators.note: putting things in order means arranging them, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: one is I in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A person can manage a hold-up by consulting a reference work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in order to' looks like plain English, but 'in order' rearranges I, CAN, COPE and DELAY.
explanation.definitionFit: An encyclopaedia is a reference work covering many subjects.
